subject: biology

items.q: In a human, a neuron and a liver cell are both descended by mitosis from the same zygote. What is the difference between them once they have differentiated?
items.correct: They express different subsets of the same complete set of genes.
items.misconception: They have kept different sets of genes and discarded the rest.
items.why: GCSE and MYP courses describe differentiation as a cell 'acquiring the structures it needs', and students merge this with the idea of 'the gene for' a particular protein, concluding that a cell must hold only the genes it uses. Talk of a cell 'losing the ability' to become other types is read as losing the genes. Differentiation is a change in gene expression, not in gene content. The unspecialized cells produced after fertilization all inherit the complete genome by mitosis; as each cell differentiates it switches on the genes for its own proteins and switches off the others, but the silent genes remain in its nucleus.
items.specStatementText: From one fertilized egg to many cell types
items.random_wrong: They were set on different paths inside from fertilization.

items.q: In an early-stage embryo a signalling protein is made by cells at one end and spreads towards the other end. Cells at three different distances from the source develop into three different cell types. Which explanation is best supported?
items.correct: Different genes are switched on above different concentrations, so each position expresses its own set.
items.misconception: The protein is an on/off switch, so the cells that received it differ from the cells that did not.
items.why: Students have met gene regulation as on/off switching, and everyday signals (a doorbell, a light switch) are binary, so they cannot see what the gradual variation of concentration in a gradient adds. The word gradient matters: the concentration changes gradually with position. Different genes are switched on at different concentration thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different combinations of genes and differentiate differently. This is how gradients have an impact on gene expression within an early-stage embryo.
items.specStatementText: From one fertilized egg to many cell types
items.random_wrong: Each cell's fate was fixed internally at fertilization; the protein only marks the region afterwards.

items.q: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?
items.correct: Capacity to divide endlessly and ability to differentiate along different pathways.
items.misconception: Ability to divide whenever a tissue is damaged and to produce more cells of its own type.
items.why: GCSE courses link cell division in adults to 'repair and replacement' and introduce stem cells in the same breath, so students file every dividing cell under stem cells, and they overlook the second defining property, differentiation along different pathways. Stem cells have two defining properties: the capacity to divide endlessly and the capacity to differentiate along different pathways. A differentiated cell that still divides, such as a fibroblast or a liver cell, has neither unlimited division nor the ability to produce other cell types, so it is not a stem cell.
items.specStatementText: What makes a cell a stem cell
items.random_wrong: Ability to switch from one specialized type to another whenever a tissue requires this.

items.q: In a hair follicle, stem cells in a region below the skin surface stay inactive for months between hair growth cycles. At the start of a new cycle they begin to divide and produce the cells of a new hair. What does this show about the stem cell niche?
items.correct: It can maintain the stem cells or activate them, according to need.
items.misconception: It stores the stem cells, which decide on their own when to begin dividing.
items.why: The everyday word niche means a recess or shelf, so students picture a storage place. Stem cells are also described as 'able to divide endlessly and become any cell', which sounds like an autonomous ability needing no outside control. A stem cell niche is a location in a tissue where the surroundings regulate the stem cells. The niche can maintain the cells, keeping them undifferentiated and quiescent, or it can promote their proliferation and differentiation when replacement cells are needed. The stem cells respond to the niche; they do not act independently of it.
items.specStatementText: Niches: where adult stem cells live and who tells them what to do
items.random_wrong: It receives fresh stem cells sent from the bone marrow when a new hair is needed.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes pluripotent stem cells from totipotent stem cells?
items.correct: Pluripotent cells can form any cell type of the body but not extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.
items.misconception: Pluripotent and totipotent cells can both form every cell type, so the two terms are interchangeable.
items.why: Both prefixes are translated as 'all' or 'many' and both terms are glossed as 'can become any cell', so the placenta and other extra-embryonic tissues, which most students have never counted as products of the embryo, are not seen as making a difference. The distinction is the extra-embryonic tissues. Cells of the very early embryo are totipotent: each can produce every cell of the embryo and of the placenta and membranes. Within a few divisions the embryonic cells become pluripotent: they can still produce any cell of the body but no longer the extra-embryonic tissues.
items.specStatementText: Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent
items.random_wrong: Pluripotent cells are the stem cells found in adult tissues such as bone marrow and hair follicles.

items.q: A cell taken from a 4-cell human embryo can develop into a complete individual with its own placenta. A cell from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst can form any tissue of the body but not a placenta. A stem cell from adult bone marrow forms only blood cells. How should the three cells be classified?
items.correct: Totipotent, then pluripotent, then finally multipotent.
items.misconception: Totipotent for both embryo cells, then multipotent.
items.why: The label 'embryonic stem cells' suggests that being embryonic is what makes a cell totipotent, and students do not picture the embryo changing during development from a few identical cells to a structured body with tissues. Cells in early-stage animal embryos are totipotent but soon become pluripotent; the pluripotent cells of the inner cell mass are the embryonic stem cells. Potency narrows as development proceeds, and the stem cells that remain in adult tissues such as bone marrow are multipotent.
items.specStatementText: Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent
items.random_wrong: Totipotent, then pluripotent for both of the others.

items.q: Which statement about the range of cell size in humans is correct?
items.correct: A motor neuron can be over a metre long, yet only micrometres wide.
items.misconception: Red and white blood cells and gametes are all about 10 µm across.
items.why: Diagrams of different specialized cells are each drawn to fill the available space with no scale bar, and the 'typical animal cell' of textbooks is a single generic size. Size is not usually presented as something that varies with function. Cell size is an aspect of specialization. The egg is large because it stores cytoplasm and nutrients for the early embryo; the sperm is tiny and streamlined for movement; red blood cells are small enough to pass through capillaries; neurons and striated muscle fibres are extremely long because their function is to carry signals or contract over a distance.
items.specStatementText: Human cells come in very different sizes
items.random_wrong: The egg and the sperm are similar in size, as each supplies half the DNA.

items.q: A cube of side 1 mm has a surface area of 6 mm², a volume of 1 mm³ and a surface area-to-volume ratio of 6. The side length is increased to 4 mm. What is the new surface area-to-volume ratio?
items.correct: 1.5, because the area becomes 96 mm² and the volume becomes 64 mm³
items.misconception: 6, because the surface area and the volume are both multiplied by four
items.why: Students apply direct proportion, the relationship they use most often, to every quantity, and do not connect area with squaring and volume with cubing when the shape is scaled up. Area depends on two lengths and volume on three, so scaling the length by a factor k multiplies the area by k² and the volume by k³. The ratio of surface area to volume is therefore multiplied by 1/k: it halves when the side is doubled.
items.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
items.random_wrong: 24, because a larger cube has more surface, so the ratio rises fourfold

items.q: A single-celled organism is growing. Why can it not keep growing indefinitely without dividing?
items.correct: Its volume, which sets its need for exchange, grows faster than the surface through which exchange occurs.
items.misconception: Its surface area-to-volume ratio rises as it grows, until the membrane cannot hold the cell together.
items.why: Students confuse the absolute surface area, which does increase with size, with the ratio of surface area to volume. Volume is less visible than surface, so its faster growth is not appreciated. For a cube of side L the surface area is 6L² and the volume L³, so the ratio is 6/L: the bigger the cube, the smaller the ratio. Although the surface area of a large cell is larger, its volume is larger by an even greater factor, so each unit of volume has less surface to serve it.
items.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
items.random_wrong: Its larger surface area increases its need for materials until supply cannot keep up with demand.

items.q: A student argues: 'Real cells are not cubes, so the cube model of surface area-to-volume ratio proves nothing about real cells.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
items.correct: The model is simplified on purpose; area and volume scale in the same way for any shape, so its conclusion holds.
items.misconception: The claim is right: a model is only valid when it has the same shape as the thing that it represents.
items.why: Students judge a model by resemblance, as they would a scale model or a picture, and have not yet separated a model's simplifying assumptions from the relationship it is built to show. Scientists deliberately simplify: a model keeps the features relevant to the question and drops the rest. The cube model keeps only size and shows that the ratio of surface area to volume falls as size increases. Because area and volume scale in the same way for spheres, cylinders or irregular cells, the conclusion is not limited to cubes.
items.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
items.random_wrong: The claim is right for another reason: in real cells the surface area and the volume grow in proportion.

items.q: A human erythrocyte has a volume of about 90 µm³ and a surface area of about 135 µm². A sphere with the same volume would have a surface area of about 97 µm². What do these figures show about the adaptation of the erythrocyte?
items.correct: Flattening gives it about 40% more surface than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds gas exchange.
items.misconception: The biconcave shape gives it about 40% more room for haemoglobin than a sphere would provide.
items.why: Students know the cell is 'packed with haemoglobin' and that its shape is special, and connect the two: the shape must be for carrying more. The dents are read as extra room rather than as lost volume. A biconcave disc has less volume, not more, than a sphere of the same width; what it gains is surface area and short diffusion distances. The adaptation is about surface area-to-volume ratio: the flattened cell exchanges gases faster because no haemoglobin molecule is far from the membrane.
items.specStatementText: Shapes that raise the ratio (HL)
items.random_wrong: The extra surface can only come from the erythrocyte being smaller than a typical sphere-shaped cell would be.

items.q: Which features of a proximal convoluted tubule cell increase its surface area-to-volume ratio, and how?
items.correct: Microvilli and basal invaginations, which add membrane area without adding volume.
items.misconception: Microvilli, which beat to sweep the filtrate across the cell so that more of it can be absorbed.
items.why: Microvilli and cilia are both drawn as small projections on the cell surface, both have Latin names for 'small hair', and students meet cilia moving mucus first, so any surface projection is assumed to move things. Microvilli are static folds of the plasma membrane supported by cytoskeleton, not motile structures. Their function is to increase surface area: the brush border of a proximal convoluted tubule cell has thousands of microvilli, giving a huge membrane area for reabsorbing glucose, ions and water from the filtrate.
items.specStatementText: Shapes that raise the ratio (HL)
items.random_wrong: A small cell size, because shape cannot alter the ratio of a cell that has a given volume.

items.q: How are type I and type II pneumocytes adapted to their functions in the alveolar epithelium?
items.correct: Type I cells are extremely thin for a short diffusion distance; type II cells hold many lamellar bodies that discharge surfactant.
items.misconception: Type II cells are the thicker gas-exchange cells; type I cells are thin cells that line the gaps between them.
items.why: Students associate activity and importance with cytoplasm and organelles, so the thicker, vesicle-rich type II cell looks like the one 'doing the work', while a thin cell looks like a passive lining. Gas exchange is by diffusion, and diffusion is fastest across short distances, so the adaptation for gas exchange is extreme thinness, which is the feature of type I pneumocytes. Type II pneumocytes are thicker precisely because they are adapted for a different job: their cytoplasm holds many lamellar bodies that discharge surfactant into the alveolar lumen.
items.specStatementText: Two pneumocytes for one job (HL)
items.random_wrong: Type I cells secrete surfactant from their lamellar bodies; type II cells are thin to allow rapid diffusion.

items.q: A striated muscle fibre has one continuous plasma membrane and cytoplasm and contains hundreds of nuclei. Which is the best assessment of whether it is a cell?
items.correct: It is debatable: one membrane and cytoplasm argue for a cell, but many nuclei and an origin by fusion argue for a syncytium.
items.misconception: It is not a cell, because a cell by definition contains exactly one nucleus, whereas this muscle fibre contains many hundreds.
items.why: The generic animal cell diagram has one nucleus and cell theory is often summarized as 'each cell has a nucleus', so the number of nuclei becomes part of the definition of a cell. Students want definitions to be clear-cut and are uncomfortable with a case that biologists themselves debate. Cell theory does not specify one nucleus per cell. The guide asks for a discussion, not a verdict: arguments for a fibre being a cell (single membrane, single cytoplasm, functions as a unit) are weighed against arguments against it (many nuclei, origin by fusion of many cells, far larger than any other cell). Both positions are defensible; what is not defensible is treating the nucleus count as settling it.
items.specStatementText: Cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres (HL)
items.random_wrong: It is a cell, because its nuclei arose by repeated mitosis inside a single cell that did not undergo cytokinesis.

items.q: A heart drug is found to block the passage of signals across the junctions where the branches of neighbouring cardiac muscle cells meet, without affecting the myofibrils inside each cell. Using the hypothesis for why cardiac muscle cells are branched, what effect on the heart wall would be predicted?
items.correct: Contraction would no longer spread through the wall in all directions, so it would not contract as a coordinated unit.
items.misconception: Contraction would still spread normally, because cardiac cells are fused into long multinucleate fibres, as in skeletal muscle.
items.why: The shared features (striations, myofibrils, contraction) are taught first and the differences later, so students generalize from skeletal muscle, the type they learn in most detail, to all striated muscle. The two types share contractile myofibrils but differ in structure. Cardiac muscle cells are short, branched and usually uninucleate, and are joined to one another where their branches meet, which is hypothesized to let contraction spread through the heart wall in every direction. Striated muscle fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleate, formed by fusion of many cells.
items.specStatementText: Cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres (HL)
items.random_wrong: Contraction would still be coordinated, because each cell is triggered by its own nerve ending, not its neighbours.

items.q: Which pairing correctly matches an adaptation of a human gamete to its function?
items.correct: Egg cytoplasm with nutrient stores: supplies the embryo's first divisions.
items.misconception: Sperm acrosome: stores the fuel that the mitochondria respire while the sperm swims.
items.why: Students learn that the egg stores nutrients and assume the sperm must have an equivalent store; the acrosome, drawn as a cap on the head, is often taken to be that store. The idea of a cell using fuel from outside itself is unfamiliar. The sperm carries almost no reserves; its head contains a haploid nucleus and an acrosome of enzymes, not fuel. ATP for the flagellum is made by mitochondria in the midpiece, which respire substrates taken up from the fluid the sperm swims in. Carrying no store keeps the cell small and light.
items.specStatementText: Sperm and egg are built for different jobs (HL)
items.random_wrong: Egg zona pellucida: a cell wall that gives the egg mechanical protection from damage.

items.q: Why do genetically identical cells in an early-stage embryo start to express different genes?
items.correct: Because they are in different positions within gradients of signalling chemicals. A cell near the source of a chemical experiences a high concentration and a cell far from it a low concentration, and the concentration a cell experiences determines which genes it switches on.
items.misconception: All the cells of an early embryo are in the same environment, so the differences between them must be programmed inside each cell from the start, independently of where the cell sits.
items.why: Diagrams of the early embryo show a ball of identical-looking cells with nothing drawn between or around them, so students assume every cell receives the same signals and that fate must be set internally, like a pre-written instruction in each cell. The embryo is not chemically uniform. Signalling chemicals are produced in particular regions and spread out, forming concentration gradients. A cell's position in a gradient sets the concentration it experiences, and that concentration influences which genes are expressed, so position in the embryo is what first makes identical cells differ.
items.specStatementText: From one fertilized egg to many cell types
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a fully differentiated cell in the human body change into a different cell type when the tissue needs it?
items.correct: In general, no. Once a cell has differentiated it keeps that identity; new cells of another type come from stem cells, which are undifferentiated and can differentiate along different pathways.
items.misconception: Specialized cells are flexible: a muscle cell or skin cell can switch to become another cell type if the body needs one, so stem cells are not really special.
items.why: News stories about reprogramming cells in the laboratory, and the fact that many plant cells can de-differentiate, are generalized to what happens naturally inside a human body. The everyday sense of 'flexible' is applied to cells. In the body, differentiation is effectively one-way for human cells: a differentiated cell keeps its structure and gene expression pattern. The capacity to produce different cell types belongs to stem cells, which are undifferentiated and can differentiate along different pathways, which is exactly why stem cells are needed in tissues throughout life.
items.specStatementText: What makes a cell a stem cell
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are stem cell niches found in an adult human?
items.correct: In several tissues that need continual replacement of cells. Bone marrow, which replaces blood cells, and hair follicles, which produce new hair, are the two examples used in this topic.
items.misconception: In adults, stem cells exist only in bone marrow, because bone marrow transplants are the stem cell treatment everyone has heard of.
items.why: Bone marrow transplants and cord blood are the stem cell stories that reach the news, so students equate adult stem cells with bone marrow and assume other tissues have none, or that other tissues must be supplied with stem cells from the marrow. Adult tissues that continually replace cells keep their own stem cells in niches. Bone marrow holds the stem cells that replace blood cells, and hair follicles hold stem cells in a region below the skin surface that produce the cells of each new hair. Each niche supplies its own tissue.
items.specStatementText: Niches: where adult stem cells live and who tells them what to do
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the stem cells in a hair follicle niche dividing all the time?
items.correct: No. Between hair growth cycles the niche maintains the stem cells in a resting, undifferentiated state; they proliferate and differentiate only when signals from the niche activate them, such as at the start of a new growth cycle.
items.misconception: Because stem cells can divide endlessly, they are always dividing, producing a constant stream of new cells whether or not the tissue needs them.
items.why: The phrase 'divide endlessly' is read as 'divide continuously', and students do not distinguish the capacity for unlimited division from the rate of division at any moment. Endless capacity to divide does not mean continuous division. A stem cell niche can maintain its stem cells in a quiescent state for long periods, and can promote their proliferation and differentiation when the tissue needs new cells. In a hair follicle the stem cells are activated at the start of each new hair growth cycle and are maintained in a resting state between cycles.
items.specStatementText: Niches: where adult stem cells live and who tells them what to do
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What range of cell types can a bone marrow stem cell produce?
items.correct: Only the different types of blood cell. Bone marrow stem cells are multipotent, not pluripotent: they cannot produce neurons, muscle cells or other cell types outside the blood.
items.misconception: Adult stem cells such as those in bone marrow are pluripotent and can be turned into any cell type, which is why they are used in medicine.
items.why: Publicity about stem cell therapies rarely distinguishes embryonic from adult stem cells, and the general description of a stem cell as able to 'become other cell types' is taken to mean any other cell type. Stem cells in adult tissues such as bone marrow are multipotent: each can differentiate into a limited range of cell types, in this case the cell types of the blood. Pluripotency, the ability to form any cell type of the body, is a property of the cells of the early embryo.
items.specStatementText: Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the size of a human egg cell compare with the size of a human sperm cell?
items.correct: The egg is very much larger. Its diameter is about 100 µm, whereas the sperm head is about 5 µm across; by volume the egg is one of the largest human cells and the sperm one of the smallest.
items.misconception: Sperm and egg cells are about the same size, because each contributes half of the genetic material to the zygote.
items.why: Fertilization is taught as an equal contribution of chromosomes from each gamete, and students carry the equality of genetic contribution over to the size of the cells. Diagrams of fertilization often show the sperm and egg at similar scales. The two gametes contribute equal numbers of chromosomes, but chromosomes occupy a tiny fraction of the egg. The egg's large size comes from its cytoplasm, which contains nutrient stores for the early embryo. The sperm carries almost no cytoplasm, so it is small and light enough to swim.
items.specStatementText: Human cells come in very different sizes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a single human cell be longer than a centimetre?
items.correct: Yes. A striated muscle fibre can be several centimetres long, and the axon of a single motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a foot muscle can be over a metre long.
items.misconception: Cells are microscopic by definition, so no cell can be long enough to see; a nerve or a muscle must be made of chains of short cells joined end to end.
items.why: Cells are introduced as things that can only be seen with a microscope, and students see nerves and muscles as visible objects, so they assume these are built from many small cells in series. Most cells are microscopic in every dimension, but neurons and striated muscle fibres are specialized by having extreme length. A single axon can extend for over a metre and a single muscle fibre for centimetres, while still being only micrometres wide. Length is one of the ways in which cell size is an aspect of specialization.
items.specStatementText: Human cells come in very different sizes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which depends on the surface area of a cell, and which on its volume: the rate at which it can exchange materials, or its need for exchange?
items.correct: The rate of exchange across the surface depends on the area of that surface, whereas the need for exchange depends on the volume of cytoplasm, because metabolism happens throughout the volume.
items.misconception: A cell's need for exchange depends on its surface area, because the surface is where substances get in and out, so a bigger surface means the cell needs more.
items.why: The membrane is where exchange is drawn and discussed, so both the supply and the demand get attached to it; students rarely think about where inside the cell the oxygen is used and the waste made. Supply and demand sit in different places. Materials cross the membrane, so the rate of exchange is limited by the area of membrane. Materials are used and produced by the cytoplasm, so the amount of exchange needed is set by the volume. As a cell grows, demand (volume) outruns supply (area), which constrains cell size.
items.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is being small the only way a cell can have a high surface area-to-volume ratio?
items.correct: No. Changing shape also raises the ratio: flattening the cell, extending the membrane into microvilli or folding it inwards (invagination) all increase surface area without increasing volume.
items.misconception: Because surface area-to-volume ratio depends on size, the only way for a cell to have a high ratio is to be small; the shape of the cell makes no difference.
items.why: The cube model varies only side length, so students take away that size is the only variable, and never see the model applied to two shapes of the same volume. The cube model holds shape constant to isolate the effect of size, but real cells can also change shape. A biconcave erythrocyte has far more surface than a sphere of the same volume, and a proximal convoluted tubule cell multiplies its membrane area with microvilli and basal invaginations while keeping the same volume.
items.specStatementText: Shapes that raise the ratio (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must all the cells in a tissue be the same type?
items.correct: No. Many tissues contain more than one cell type because different adaptations are needed for the overall function; the alveolar epithelium contains both type I and type II pneumocytes.
items.misconception: A tissue is a group of identical cells working together, so every cell in a tissue is the same type.
items.why: The GCSE and MYP definition of a tissue as 'a group of similar cells with the same function' is remembered as 'identical cells', and the diagrams of tissues that accompany it show rows of one cell type. A tissue can contain several cell types when its overall function needs adaptations that cannot all be built into one cell. Gas exchange needs the extreme thinness of type I pneumocytes, and surfactant secretion needs cells with many lamellar bodies, so both type I and type II pneumocytes are present in the alveolar epithelium.
items.specStatementText: Two pneumocytes for one job (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a striated muscle fibre come to contain many nuclei?
items.correct: It is formed during development by the fusion of many separate cells (myoblasts), each contributing its nucleus to the shared cytoplasm.
items.misconception: The nucleus of a muscle cell divides many times without the cell dividing, so the cell fills up with nuclei.
items.why: Students know that nuclei are produced by mitosis, and that mitosis is normally followed by cytokinesis, so the simplest explanation for many nuclei in one cell is mitosis without cytokinesis. The idea of separate cells fusing is unfamiliar. Striated muscle fibres are multinucleate because they arise by fusion of many myoblasts, not by repeated nuclear division within one cell. This origin is the reason for the debate over whether a fibre is a cell: it has one continuous plasma membrane and cytoplasm, but it was formed from many cells.
items.specStatementText: Cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the layer around a human egg cell, outside its plasma membrane?
items.correct: The zona pellucida, a layer of glycoproteins secreted around the egg. It is not a cell wall: a sperm's acrosome releases enzymes that digest a path through it, and after fertilization the contents of the egg's cortical granules alter it so that no further sperm can enter.
items.misconception: The egg is surrounded by a cell wall, which protects it and which the sperm has to break through.
items.why: Students know that plant cells have a wall outside the membrane and that bird eggs have a shell, so a protective layer outside an animal cell's membrane is called a wall by analogy. The word 'penetrate' used for sperm entry reinforces the image of a rigid barrier. Animal cells, including the egg, have no cell wall. The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein coat that sperm bind to and digest through with acrosome enzymes; it is then modified by cortical granule contents to block further sperm. It is a specialized adaptation of the egg, not a cell wall.
items.specStatementText: Sperm and egg are built for different jobs (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the surface area-to-volume ratio of a cell calculated?
items.correct: Surface area divided by volume. For a cube of side 4 mm, 96 mm² / 64 mm³ = 1.5 mm⁻¹.
items.misconception: The ratio can be worked out either way round, or is volume divided by surface area, since a ratio just compares the two numbers.
items.why: Students meet ratios written as 'a : b' without a fixed order, and the phrase 'ratio between volume and surface area' in everyday use does not tell them which number is the numerator, so they divide the larger by the smaller or the first-named by the second. The quantity is defined as surface area divided by volume, because the question it answers is how much surface serves each unit of volume. Inverting it gives a number that rises with size and hides the constraint on cell growth. Always write surface area first and check that the ratio falls as the cell gets bigger.
items.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the signal to contract pass from one cardiac muscle cell to the next through the heart wall?
items.correct: Directly from cell to cell across the junctions where the branches of neighbouring cells meet. Because each branched cell is joined to several neighbours, the signal and the contraction spread through the wall in all directions and the wall contracts as a coordinated unit.
items.misconception: Each cardiac muscle cell is made to contract by its own nerve ending, so cardiac cells do not need to be connected to one another to contract together.
items.why: Skeletal muscle, which students meet first, contracts when a motor neuron stimulates each fibre, and students generalize this to all muscle. Knowing that nerves speed up or slow down the heart reinforces the idea that nerves trigger every contraction of every cell. Cardiac muscle cells are joined where their branches meet, and the signal to contract passes from cell to cell across these junctions. The hypothesis for branching is that it lets this signal, and the contraction, spread through the whole wall in every direction; nerves adjust the rate but do not stimulate each cell separately. Cells that could not pass the signal to their neighbours would not contract in a coordinated way.
items.specStatementText: Cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres (HL)

items.q: Is branching of cardiac muscle cells an adaptation for increasing surface area-to-volume ratio?
items.correct: No. The hypothesis for branching is that it lets each cell connect with several neighbours, so that contraction spreads through the heart wall in all directions; it is an adaptation for coordination, not for exchange of materials.
items.misconception: Cardiac muscle cells are branched to increase their surface area-to-volume ratio, so that the hard-working heart muscle can take up oxygen faster.
items.why: Flattening, microvilli and invagination have just been taught as shape changes that raise surface area-to-volume ratio, so students apply the same explanation to every unusual cell shape, and the heart's high oxygen demand makes the explanation sound convincing. The branches are the sites where cardiac cells join their neighbours, and their significance is that the signal to contract, and the contraction itself, can spread through the network in every direction. Oxygen supply to cardiac cells depends on the dense capillary network around them, not on the branched shape; branching is hypothesized to serve coordinated contraction of the wall.
